title: How Well Do LLMs Write Infrastructure Modules? iac-bench 2026-10 Results
summary: We asked ten language models to write reusable OpenTofu modules for AWS, GCP and Azure, then scored 90 modules against real plans and a calibrated judge. Here is how they did and the patterns behind the scores.
body_markdown:
**iac-bench release 2026-10 · run 2026-10-22 · 10 models · 3 clouds · 90 attempts**


We asked ten language models to write reusable OpenTofu modules for three common cloud services intended for a specific audience:


- an S3 bucket for application teams (AWS);
- a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for a DBA team (GCP);
- an App Service web app for an SRE team (Azure).


Each request was a few sentences describing the high level use case of the module and the intended audience. We never listed the specific security, durability or hygiene requirements a senior reviewer would expect.


We scored the 90 resulting modules on two components:


- **Mechanical rubric (70%).** Fixture-specific checks evaluated against real` tofu plan` output.
- **Judge (30%).** A calibrated LLM judge grading design and craft against a published quality doctrine.


This article reports the results and the patterns behind them:


- [Methodology](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-methodology) : how it was done.
- [Scoring criteria](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-scoring-criteria) : the reference for every criterion ID used below.
- Per-model reports : one page per model.


## Key findings


1. **Four models form a top group:** Claude Opus 5.5 (88.9), Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Sonnet 5.5, all between 86.1 and 88.9.


- All four have 95% rank intervals within 1–5. The models ranked below them reach fifth at best, except Claude Haiku 5.5, whose interval (1–9) is widened by two failed attempts.
- Within the group, Claude Opus 5.5 is the most dependable: no failed gates, no security findings, and the highest floor in the field. Its weakest attempt scored 85.0. Its lead is not statistically decisive.


2. **Universal blind spots, regardless of vendor or rank:**


- **S3 logging permission (G001` H13` ).** No attempt, out of 30, gave the S3 logging service permission to deliver access logs.
- **Database drops (G002` H11` ).** 24 of the 28 Cloud SQL modules that planned drop a database's data when it is removed from the module's input.
- **Provider version bounds (` B1` ).** Constraints admitting the next major version appear in 19/30 AWS modules and 22/28 GCP modules. Only 2/28 Azure modules did this.


3. **Security failures come in two forms,** and different models fall into different ones.


- 25 of 90 attempts failed a mandatory security item.
- In 15, a security setting was exposed as a consumer input, usually with a safe default.
- In the other 10, a setting the provider defaults insecurely was never set.
- Four models had no security findings: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna.


4. **The ranking does not depend on the LLM judge.** Ranked by the mechanical score alone, the ten models fall in exactly the same order as the composite. The judge reorders models only within its own component, and it catches defects the rubric cannot see (and the reverse).
5. **Cost buys little at the top.**


- **Most expensive:** Claude Fable 5.1, at about $14 for nine attempts.
- **Similar scores for less:** Claude Opus 5.5 ($3.58) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($1.52).
- **Cheapest:** GPT-6 Luna scores 81.5 for five cents in total, with no security findings.


6. **Open weights trail the leaders but sit mid-field.**


- Kimi K3 places fifth (82.4), ahead of GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 3.1 Pro.
- DeepSeek V4 Pro places eighth.

Composite = 0.70 × mechanical + 0.30 × judge. Fixture columns are medians of three attempts. ✗ = attempts whose module did not plan; ⚠ = attempts failing at least one mandatory security item. Costs are estimates at list prices on 2026-10-23 and exclude judging.


*Figure 1. Overall composite (mean of the three per-fixture medians). Whiskers show the bootstrap 95% CI; the right-hand labels give the 95% rank interval.*


**How to read the ranking.** Three samples per model per fixture is enough to separate groups but not neighbors:


- **Top group:** Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Sonnet 5.5. Their rank intervals overlap.
- **Clearest separation:** Claude Opus 5.5 is the only model whose interval (1–3) stays within the top three.
- **Bottom:** Gemini 3.6 Flash ranks last in at least 95% of bootstrap draws.
- **Middle:** the remaining models overlap one another.


Claude Haiku 5.5's interval is the widest in the release. It is driven by one fixture where two of three modules failed to plan. Pairwise win probabilities are in the data release.


## Results by fixture


*Figure 2. Median composite of three attempts, per model and fixture.*


Fixture Field median Best median Most-missed rubric item (attempts that planned) Most-missed mandatory item


G001 · S3 81.8 87.9 (Claude Opus 5.5)` H13` log delivery permitted: 30/30 missed` H1` public access block: 6/30


G002 · Cloud SQL 82.2 91.3 (GPT-6 Astra)` H11` databases dropped on removal: 24/28` H2` encrypted connections: 9/28


G003 · App Service 86.2 95.9 (GPT-6 Astra)` A7` interface budget: 19/28` H2` basic-auth publishing: 10/28


Fixture scores are not interchangeable. **G001 (S3)** punishes omission: the brief's audience is developers who "don't know S3 well," so every hygiene decision falls to the module. The models that lose the most here:


- GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna build secure but minimal buckets, with no lifecycle rules and no access logging. That costs them up to a quarter of the rubric.
- Gemini 3.6 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Pro expose the public access block as an input.


**G002 (Cloud SQL)** rewards locking down a specialist's interface without taking their controls away. **G003 (App Service)** depends heavily on two settings the Azure provider leaves insecure by default.


## Finding 1: The same blind spots, across vendors


Some criteria were missed by nearly every model, regardless of vendor, size or overall rank. These are the clearest signal in the release, because they do not depend on which model you pick.


*Figure 3. Share of attempts earning full credit on the rubric items most often missed, by model. Item definitions are in[Scoring criteria](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-scoring-criteria) .*


These criteria were missed by most of the field.


**Access logs that cannot be delivered (G001` H13` , 30/30 missed).**


- Nineteen S3 attempts offered no server access logging at all (` H9` ).
- The rest point logging at a target bucket but never grant the S3 logging service permission to write to it, so S3 cannot deliver any logs.
- Every model, in every attempt, missed this.


**Databases dropped when removed from the input (G002` H11` , 24/28 missed).**


- ` google_sql_database` defaults to deleting the database, and its data, when the resource is removed.
- A DBA who removes a name from a module's` databases` list therefore drops that database's data on the next apply.
- Only GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.1 Pro and DeepSeek V4 Pro guarded against this, and only in some attempts, by setting` deletion_policy = "ABANDON"` or tying it to deletion protection.


**Backups that cannot be turned off (G002` H4` /` H5` ).** This one splits by rank:


- **The top models:** hardcode automated backups and point-in-time recovery to always on. That is safe, but it gives a DBA no way to skip backups on a disposable test instance, so it earns partial credit.
- **The full-credit attempts:** only Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and the two Gemini models shipped backups on by default with a real opt-out.
- **Backups that outlive the instance:** no attempt kept automated backups after instance deletion (G002` E1` , 0/28). By default Cloud SQL deletes them with the instance.


**Provider constraints that admit the next major version (` B1` ).**


Cloud Attempts with such a constraint


AWS 19/30


GCP 22/28


Azure 2/28


- **AWS and GCP:** the typical forms are an open-ended` >= 5.0` , or a window such as` >= 5.0, < 7.0` that spans two majors.
- **Azure:** modules almost always used` ~> 4.0` .


The habit looks provider-specific rather than model-specific: the same models that bound` azurerm` correctly left` aws` and` google` open.


**Expertise that only a few models showed:**


- **Cloud SQL login role** (` roles/cloudsql.instanceUser` , G002` E6` ): 13/28 granted it for the IAM database users they created. Without it, those users cannot log in.
- **Cloud SQL connection logging** (G002` E8` ): 12/28.
- **Key Vault references on App Service** (G003` E5` ): 6/28.


## Finding 2: Two ways to ship an insecure module


*Figure 4. Attempts with at least one mandatory security failure, and attempts that did not plan, out of 9 per model.*


Each fixture has two **mandatory** items: its most severe security failures. Twenty-five of 90 attempts failed at least one.


Pattern Attempts What it looks like Models


**Secure default, open override** 15 The secure value is the default, but the setting is an input any consumer can change. For example,` ssl_mode` defaults to` ENCRYPTED_ONLY` while the validation also accepts` ALLOW_UNENCRYPTED_AND_ENCRYPTED` . Gemini 3.6 Flash, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro


**Insecure provider default left in place** 10 The module never sets the attribute, and the provider's default is insecure. On Azure, basic-auth publishing for FTP and Web Deploy is on unless disabled. Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, plus some attempts by DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.6 Flash


**Secure default, open override.** The doctrine treats this as a defect even when the default is safe. A module's security posture has to hold for every consumer, and an input that can silently weaken it will eventually be used to do so. Models in this pattern often document the risk in the same breath: one description reads "Do not weaken this without a security review" above a validation list that allows exactly that.


**Insecure provider default left in place.** This failure cannot be seen by reading the source, because nothing is written down. The most-missed mandatory item in the release is G003` H2` (basic-auth publishing, 10/28). Several of these modules set HTTPS-only, TLS 1.2 and FTPS-off correctly in the same block, and still miss the two publishing flags the Azure provider enables by default.


**Failed gates.** Four attempts produced modules that did not plan:


- **Two Claude Haiku 5.5 Cloud SQL attempts:** each looked up a network inside a placeholder project, saw` tofu plan` fail, and submitted anyway.
- **One Kimi K3 App Service attempt:** the deployment slot is missing a provider-required attribute.
- **One Gemini 3.6 Flash App Service attempt:** its outputs reference a resource that the module never declares.


## Finding 3: The rubric and the judge catch different defects, and the ranking holds without either


*Figure 5. Mechanical-only and judge-only scores per model (mean of per-fixture medians).*


**The ranking holds without the judge.** Ranked by the mechanical score alone, the ten models fall in exactly the composite order. The judge's 30% shifts scores but never reorders the leaderboard.


Model Mechanical only Judge only Composite rank


Claude Opus 5.5 86.4 (#1) 94.7 (#1) 1


Claude Fable 5.1 85.0 (#2) 91.2 (#5) 2


GPT-6 Astra 83.2 (#3) 94.7 (#2) 3


Claude Sonnet 5.5 82.5 (#4) 94.7 (#3) 4


Kimi K3 80.6 (#5) 86.0 (#6) 5


GPT-6 Luna 79.7 (#6) 84.2 (#7) 6


Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.9 (#7) 71.9 (#8) 7


DeepSeek V4 Pro 69.5 (#8) 67.5 (#9) 8


Claude Haiku 5.5 59.2 (#9) 91.2 (#4) 9


Gemini 3.6 Flash 50.9 (#10) 62.3 (#10) 10


The two components disagree on individual modules, and the disagreements are systematic.


**What the judge misses.** It reads source, so it cannot see:


- an insecure provider default that the source never mentions. It gave the App Service attempts with basic-auth findings full marks on *Anti-patterns* for their hardcoded HTTPS and TLS settings;
- a module that does not plan. It graded the four failed-gate modules between 50 and 89.5.


**What the rubric misses.** It checks planned outcomes, so it cannot see:


- whether documentation is true;
- whether an input is ever wired to anything;
- whether a collection input breaks the plan once it is populated.


The judge scored *Documentation* 0 in 26 of 90 attempts. It found, for example, a databases input that fails as soon as one database is declared, which the rubric credited.


**Disagreement about restraint.** The largest single gap is GPT-6 Astra on S3:


- **Rubric:** about 64. It charges for every data-hygiene item missing from a bucket that never expires anything.
- **Judge:** 94.7. It credits the same bucket as restrained.


A reader who rejects the rubric's view can read the judge-only column, and the reverse.


**Self-preference.** The judge is Claude Opus 5.5. Claude models take three of the top four judge-only ranks, alongside GPT-6 Astra. But the composite order, and Claude Opus 5.5's first place, are identical under the mechanical score alone, where no model judges any other.


## Finding 4: Cost and capability are only loosely related


*Figure 6. Overall composite against the estimated cost of one attempt at each fixture, at list prices on 2026-10-23. The dashed line is the Pareto frontier: models no other model beats on both cost and score.*


Generation cost varies by a factor of about 280 across the field, and it is only loosely related to score.

The Pareto frontier, the models no other model beats on both cost and score, runs through:


- **GPT-6 Luna:** the cheapest model with no security findings.
- **Claude Sonnet 5.5:** the cheapest model in the top group.
- **Claude Opus 5.5:** the highest score.


Claude Fable 5.1 costs about four times as much as Claude Opus 5.5 for a slightly lower score. Claude Haiku 5.5 is the second-cheapest model and would sit near the frontier, but for its two failed Cloud SQL attempts.


Costs are estimates: token counts multiplied by list prices. They exclude judging and any provider-specific caching discounts beyond a flat cache-read and cache-write multiplier.


## Finding 5: Documentation is where good modules lose points


*Documentation* is the judged section most often scored 0: in 26 of 90 attempts. Nearly every module has documentation. The zeros come from **documentation that is wrong** :


- a description that promises behavior the code does not implement;
- a stated limit that disagrees with the service;
- a comment contradicted by the line below it.


Under the doctrine, any wrong statement scores 0, however small.


Pattern Examples


Limits misstated 1–35 days of WAL retention described for an edition that allows 1–7


Inverted meaning A deletion-protection input described as "whether or not to allow Terraform to destroy the instance"


Features that do not exist "Least-requests load balancing" that is never configured; a staging-traffic input that feeds only an output


**Longer documentation produces more of these errors.** The models that write long READMEs (Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, Kimi K3) give the judge more claims to check:


- GPT-6 Astra had no zero.
- DeepSeek V4 Pro had six, one in every Cloud SQL and App Service attempt.
- Claude Haiku 5.5 had five.


## Finding 6: One sample is not enough


**The same model, prompt and fixture can produce very different modules.** Nine of the 30 model-fixture cells spread by more than 10 points across their three attempts. Four spread by more than 20:


Model · fixture Range Cause


Claude Haiku 5.5 · Cloud SQL 25.3–91.0 Two attempts did not plan


Kimi K3 · App Service 25.3–89.4 One attempt did not plan


Gemini 3.6 Flash · App Service 15.0–62.4 One attempt did not plan


DeepSeek V4 Pro · App Service 57.8–81.8 Basic-auth flags set in one attempt, absent in two


Two consequences:


- **Single-sample leaderboards are fragile.** A single draw would have put Claude Haiku 5.5 anywhere from first to ninth.
- **Consistency is itself a capability.** It separates the top group as much as peak quality does.


Every model in the top group has all three attempts within 11 points on every fixture. Claude Opus 5.5's widest spread is 8.5 points.

## Limitations


The main limitations of this release:


- **Plan-only.** Nothing was applied, so errors that only appear at apply time are not measured.
- **Three fixtures.** Results should not be generalized beyond these three services.
- **Three attempts per cell.** Neighboring models usually cannot be separated.
- **Undated model aliases.** Results are tied to the run date (2026-10-22).
- **A single judge from the same vendor as four candidates.** Mitigated by calibration and by reporting the mechanical score alone, not eliminated.
- **An opinionated doctrine.** Massdriver, which builds infrastructure tooling, wrote the briefs, rubrics and doctrine.


Full discussion:[Methodology §7–8](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-methodology#7-limitations) .
